title: Banks on notice as Australians consult AI to help choose their lender
full_text:
For many years, prospective bank customers have used a search engine like Google to help them decide who to borrow from. These days, it’s more likely they will have conversed with artificial intelligence for guidance.
For banks and fintechs, that means efforts to make their brand more visible to search algorithms, a strategy known as search engine optimisation, are no longer enough. A new approach is required to ensure their name pops up in answers delivered by large language models such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude.
The new techniques, sometimes known as “generative engine optimisation”, are set to have a major impact on lending volumes across the finance sector. Customers will discover borrowing options by talking to AI through different stages of the product journey, from education to exploration, evaluation and selection.
“It’s like being back in 1998 before the internet came out, before Google existed. That’s where we’re at,” said Jeremy Liddle, executive chair of Third Hemisphere. “But we’re going to go through five years of what happened in the dotcom era in the next six to 12 months.”
His firm is developing a series of ‘AI authority’ indexes to show where and how brands appear in AI-generated responses to questions such as ‘which credit card lenders are best and worst?’ or ‘what is the best mortgage product?’
“AI SEO is being invented right now. It’s the wild west. And the companies that invest in it early will be light years in front when AI agents actively start making decisions on behalf of buyers,” Liddle said.
In each conversation with its user, an AI model scours the internet for brand sentiment in seconds. It ingests content including media articles, comparison sites, lists of awards, customer reviews on social media and company webpages, forming a picture presented to the customer as a natural conversation.
Third Hemisphere’s AI authority index for personal lending collected over 154,791 answers, after asking 166 questions across five engines: ChatGPT, Claude, Google’s Gemini, Microsoft’s Copilot and Perplexity.
Scores were allocated based on how consistently a lender was named, combining reputation, influence, presence and the readability for AI of corporate websites.
Commonwealth Bank was the clear winner in searches for personal loans, including credit cards, while ANZ was a laggard among the big four. ING and fintechs like OurMoneyMarket, Plenti and Harmoney scored ahead of NAB, Westpac, Macquarie and ANZ on reputation.
One of the challenges of AI search is customers using more nuanced and subjective questions than traditional search: for example, ‘which credit card can I trust, and who should I avoid’ or ‘I have a bad credit rating and I want to consolidate my debt, which lenders are best and worst?’ This forces the models to look for positive and negative views.
“Using Gemini or Grok on your phone is becoming the starting point in the buying journey,” said Dan Jones, who leads the digital practice at consultancy firm Oliver Wyman.
“Customers are using compare and contrast prompts and asking for pros and cons of doing something – and there is a big difference in how banks are showing up in large language model results.
“This is an opportunity to get clever on how a product works and to articulate simpler terms and conditions to capture attention. Banks also need to make it easier to move to the next step, when the customer asks: what do I do next?”
The models look for unbiased information with authority. CBA’s strong showing could be driven by its recent decision to expand its corporate news pages on its website, which is producing multiple articles a day on topics across economics, technology, business innovation, and regional and community initiatives. This helps the AI models see it as a trusted source of information beyond its own products.
Models can use different sources for negative information. Claude, for example, relies on Financial Counselling Australia’s Rank the Banks survey when a customer asks it “who should I avoid?” while ChatGPT favours ASIC enforcement actions.
Six of the lenders in Third Hemisphere’s index were rated “off the guest list”, reflecting a low reputation score and low internet presence. They were St George, Cash Converters, Bank of Queensland, Latitude Financial Services, Nimble and Resimac.
Buy now, pay later lenders also fared relatively poorly, with Afterpay, Zip, Klarna and neobank Revolut rated “under the radar” (not named in many answers).
AI will also create challenges for comparison firms. According to the analysis, the most authoritative sites, in order, are: Canstar, Finder, Money.com.au, Mozo, Savings.com.au, Forbes Advisor, InfoChoice, Your Mortgage, LoanOptions.ai, ClearScore, Savvy and RateCity.
Third Hemisphere is developing similar indexes for mortgages, business lending, superannuation, managed funds and wealth and, beyond financial services, energy and telecommunications.
Ensuring brands appear in AI answers will become more important if financial AI agents take off. Meta Muse, not yet available in Australia, can work as a financial assistant doing basic banking and selecting products.
As more AI bots search for reputation in real-time and weigh this up against historical sources, the public relations game will also change.
“For any listed company, a big proportion of total enterprise value is tied up in goodwill,” said Tony Surtees, a technology entrepreneur and investor who has set up a new reputation intelligence company, Contrlr, with Liddle.
“You need to be constantly surveilling and creating a common base of intelligence to understand how your sentiment is actually being affected on an hour-by-hour basis; and how, when necessary, you need to intervene,” Surtees said.
